source: School Science curriculum journey 2026–27 (Year 11 Term 1: Organic Chemistry; Astrophysics) with Edexcel GCSE Biology Topic 9 (ecosystems and material cycles); school's Pearson Edexcel GCSE 5-year schemes; INSET lesson standard. Orbital-speed, red-shift-equation and HR-diagram content goes beyond GCSE 1PH0 and is marked as stretch. | Edexcel IGCSE 4BI1/4CH1 specification summary (content/syllabus/ks4/gcse-science.json), Y11 units Biology 3, Biology 4, Biology 5, Chemistry 3, Chemistry 4. Drive material not used. Not re-taught because covered by the existing lessons in content/lessons/gcse-science/y11.json: population, community, habitat, ecosystem and quadrats; biotic and abiotic factors; food chains, webs and pyramids and 10% energy transfer; carbon cycle; nitrogen cycle with named bacteria; pollution (sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, greenhouse gases, sewage and eutrophication) and deforestation (Biology 4 points 1, 3-7); hydrocarbons, formulae and homologous series, crude oil and fractional distillation, complete and incomplete combustion and acid rain, catalytic cracking, alkane and alkene reactions with the bromine water test, addition polymers (Chemistry 4 points 1 partly, 2-6, 8). Biology 4 biodiversity and distribution (point 2) and Chemistry 4 naming and isomers (point 1) are taught here. | Edexcel IGCSE Physics 4PH1 specification (units Physics 5-8, Y11). Existing UK-GCSE lessons in content/lessons/gcse-science/y11.json already cover Physics 8 gravity and the Solar System, g on other bodies, orbital speed (v = 2 pi r / T), life cycles of stars, colour and temperature, absolute magnitude and the HR diagram, red-shift and the CMB, so Physics 8 here adds orbits of comets and satellites and one consolidation lesson in exam terms.

lessons.title: Human reproduction, the menstrual cycle and the placenta
lessons.bigQuestion: How does the body prepare, protect and nourish a new life?
objectives: Describe the structure and functions of the male and female reproductive systems
Describe the roles of oestrogen and progesterone and the menstrual cycle
Describe the placenta and the secondary sexual characteristics
successCriteria: All: name parts of the reproductive systems and their functions
Most: describe the menstrual cycle and placenta
Some: interpret hormone graphs and explain pregnancy
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: relationships and sex education (follow the school's RSE policy)
lessons.smsc: Moral: modesty (haya), respect, responsibility; gratitude for the gift of life

keywords.def: release of an egg from the ovary
organ where substances are exchanged between mother and fetus
attachment of the embryo to the uterus lining
features that develop at puberty, controlled by sex hormones

starter: Bismillah. What does a hormone do?
Name the process by which a sperm and egg join.

teach.heading: The systems
bullets: Male: testes make sperm and testosterone
Female: ovaries make eggs, oestrogen, progesterone
Sperm travel in the sperm duct; egg moves along the oviduct
teach.note: Teach factually and respectfully; follow the school's RSE guidance and the parental policy. Fertilisation takes place in the oviduct. The zygote divides to form an embryo that implants in the uterus lining. Gestation is about 40 weeks.

head: Part
Function
rows: makes and releases eggs; oestrogen and progesterone
carries the egg; fertilisation happens here
where the embryo implants and develops

teach.heading: The menstrual cycle
bullets: About 28 days; ovulation around day 14
Oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining
Progesterone maintains the lining after ovulation
teach.note: If no fertilisation occurs, progesterone falls and the lining breaks down (menstruation, days 1 to 5). If fertilisation occurs the lining is kept and the cycle pauses. Other hormones (FSH, LH) control the ovary; they are not required for all pupils, so check the specification.

teach.heading: Placenta and pregnancy
bullets: Large surface area with villi; thin barrier
Oxygen and nutrients to fetus; CO₂ and urea to mother
Blood of mother and fetus do not mix
teach.note: Amniotic fluid cushions the fetus. The placenta is selective, but alcohol, nicotine and some viruses (e.g. rubella) can cross it; this is why pregnant women are advised to avoid these.

model.problem: Explain why progesterone stays high in early pregnancy. [2 marks]
steps: Progesterone maintains the thick lining of the uterus
If it fell, the lining would break down
model.answer: It keeps the uterus lining in place so the embryo can develop

teach.heading: Puberty and hormones
bullets: Testosterone: deeper voice, facial hair, muscle
Oestrogen: breast development, wider hips, periods
Controlled by the pituitary gland sending signals
teach.note: Keep language age-appropriate and accurate. These are secondary sexual characteristics; the primary sexual characteristics are the sex organs.

misconception.wrong: Hormones travel along nerves to reach the target organ.
misconception.right: Hormones are carried in the blood plasma to their target organs.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils think fertilisation happens in the uterus.

check.q: Where does fertilisation normally take place in humans?
check.why: The sperm meets the egg in the oviduct. The embryo then moves to the uterus to implant.

practice: Name the hormone made in the testes.
State two substances that pass from fetus to mother across the placenta.
What happens to the uterus lining if no fertilisation occurs?

lessons.title: DNA, genes, the genome and protein synthesis
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a four-letter code build every protein in your body?
objectives: Describe the structure of DNA and the terms genome, gene, chromosome
Describe RNA and complementary base pairing
Describe transcription and translation in protein synthesis
successCriteria: All: describe the double helix and base pairing
Most: use base pairing to write complementary strands
Some: explain transcription and translation and how mutations affect proteins
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: bonding and polymers; Computing: coding
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the order in the code of life

keywords.def: all the genetic material of an organism
section of DNA that codes for a protein
three bases that code for one amino acid
messenger RNA copied from DNA that carries the code to the ribosome

starter: Bismillah. Where is DNA found in a human cell?

teach.heading: DNA and chromosomes
bullets: DNA is a double helix of two strands
Bases pair: A with T, C with G
The genome is all of an organism's DNA
teach.note: Each nucleotide has a phosphate, sugar and base. The human genome has about 3 billion base pairs and about 20 000 protein-coding genes. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes in the nucleus. Chromosomes are long coiled DNA with many genes.

model.problem: One DNA strand reads ATG CCA GTT. Write the complementary strand. If 20% of bases in a DNA sample are adenine, what are the percentages of the others?
steps: A pairs with T, C pairs with G
ATG CCA GTT pairs with TAC GGT CAA
model.answer: TAC GGT CAA; T 20%, C 30%, G 30%

teach.heading: RNA
bullets: Single-stranded, shorter than DNA
Sugar is ribose; uracil (U) replaces thymine
Types include messenger RNA (mRNA)
teach.note: Compare with DNA: DNA double-stranded in the nucleus; RNA single-stranded and can leave the nucleus. U pairs with A.

teach.heading: Making a protein
bullets: Transcription: mRNA copies a gene in the nucleus
mRNA moves to a ribosome
Translation: amino acids joined in the order coded by codons
teach.note: Transfer RNA brings amino acids. Each codon codes for one amino acid, e.g. UUU for phenylalanine. The order of amino acids decides the folding and shape, and shape decides function (enzyme active site).
cycle: Amino acids join to make a protein

teach.heading: A mistake in the code
bullets: A mutation changes the DNA base sequence
May change amino acid order
Protein shape and function may change
teach.note: Link to enzymes and cystic fibrosis: a change in one gene may lead to an enzyme or transport protein that does not fold correctly. Not every mutation changes the protein (the code has some redundancy).

misconception.wrong: Each gene makes a whole cell.
misconception.right: A gene codes for one protein. The cell's features come from many proteins working together.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils say T pairs with A in RNA; in RNA uracil pairs with A.

check.q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
check.why: RNA has uracil (U) instead of thymine (T).

practice: Write the complementary DNA strand to CGA TTC.
State where translation takes place.
Define gene and genome.
independent: Core: Draw a flow chart of protein synthesis.
Extend: The mRNA sequence is AUG CCA GUU. Write the DNA template strand that formed it. [2 marks]
Stretch: Explain how a mutation in a gene could cause an enzyme to stop working. [4 marks]
exit: State two differences between DNA and RNA. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: describe how the code becomes a protein.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph on how a gene becomes a protein, using at least six key terms.

lessons.title: Alleles and monohybrid crosses
lessons.bigQuestion: If both parents are tall, can a child be short?
objectives: Use the terms allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype and phenotype
Complete Punnett squares for monohybrid crosses
Describe codominance (Biology only)
successCriteria: All: define the key terms
Most: complete crosses and give ratios and probabilities
Some: explain codominance and work out parent genotypes from offspring
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: probability and ratio
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness and respect for the diversity in people

keywords.def: a different version of a gene
combination of alleles an organism has
the observable characteristic
both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote

starter: State the number of chromosomes in a human gamete.

teach.heading: Genetic vocabulary
bullets: Dominant allele shows in the heterozygote
Recessive allele shows only if there are two copies
Homozygous: two identical alleles; heterozygous: two different
teach.note: Use capital letter for dominant (T) and lower case for recessive (t). Genotype is the letters, phenotype is the visible trait. A pea plant Tt is tall; tt is dwarf.

teach.heading: Model: monohybrid cross
bullets: Write parent genotypes and gametes
Fill the Punnett square
State ratio and probability
teach.note: Tt × Tt: gametes T, t from each parent. Offspring: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Phenotypes 3 tall : 1 dwarf. Probability of dwarf = 1 in 4 (25%). Also show Tt × tt giving 1 : 1.

model.problem: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt) are crossed. Give the genotype ratio, phenotype ratio and probability of a dwarf plant.
steps: Gametes: T or t from each parent
Square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt

teach.heading: Codominance (Biology only)
bullets: Both alleles are fully expressed
ABO blood group: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant
Iᴼ is recessive to both
teach.note: Use letters I with superscripts A, B and O. Genotype IAIB gives group AB. Example: IAIO × IBIO gives A, B, AB or O in equal 1 in 4 chances.

misconception.wrong: The dominant allele is always the more common allele in a population.
misconception.right: Dominant means it shows in the heterozygote. It need not be the most common.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils say 100% because both parents are dominant phenotype; heterozygous parents can have recessive offspring.

check.q: Two heterozygous parents (Bb) have a child. What is the probability the child is bb?
check.why: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb, so one in four is bb.

practice: Define homozygous and heterozygous.
Give the phenotype of Tt where T is tall and dominant.
Complete a cross between Tt and tt.
independent: Core: Complete a Punnett square for Bb × Bb where B = brown eyes and b = blue eyes.
Extend: Parents with blood groups IAIO and IBIO: list the possible groups of their children. [3 marks]
Stretch: A tall plant crossed with a dwarf produces 48 tall and 52 dwarf offspring. Deduce the parent genotypes. [3 marks]
exit: Explain why two tall parents can have a short child. [3 marks]
Return to the big question using genotype language.
lessons.homework: Complete three crosses with Punnett squares and ratios.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: gamete cards to physically build squares. Stretch: what is a test cross?

lessons.title: Pedigrees, inherited disorders and sex determination
lessons.bigQuestion: Can we predict who will inherit a family condition?
objectives: Interpret family pedigrees and deduce genotypes
Explain inheritance of cystic fibrosis and Huntington's disease
Explain sex determination with XX and XY
successCriteria: All: describe sex determination
Most: interpret a simple pedigree
Some: calculate probabilities for carriers and future children
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: probability
lessons.smsc: Moral: compassion and respect for people with genetic conditions

keywords.def: a person who has one copy of a recessive allele but does not show the condition
family tree showing inheritance of a trait
X and Y chromosomes that determine sex
recessive disorder causing thick mucus in the lungs

starter: Bismillah. Cross Aa × Aa and give the ratio.
How many chromosomes in a human body cell?

teach.heading: Sex determination
bullets: Females XX, males XY
Egg always carries X
Sperm carries X or Y: the sperm decides the sex
teach.note: A Punnett square gives 50% female and 50% male on average. Each pregnancy is independent, so a family with three girls has a 50% chance of a boy next. Probability of three girls in a row is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

teach.heading: Reading a pedigree
bullets: Squares male, circles female; shaded affected
Two unaffected parents with an affected child: recessive
Affected parents with unaffected child: dominant
teach.note: Describe: Parents are unaffected; of their four children, one daughter and one son have cystic fibrosis. Each unaffected parent must carry one recessive allele (Cc). A third unaffected child has a 2 in 3 chance of being a carrier.

model.problem: Both parents are unaffected. Their first child has cystic fibrosis (cc). Explain the parents' genotypes and the probability that their next child is affected.
steps: The child has cc: one c from each parent
Parents are unaffected so they must be Cc (carriers)
Cc × Cc gives CC, Cc, Cc, cc

teach.heading: Two inherited disorders
bullets: Cystic fibrosis: recessive, thick mucus in lungs and gut
Huntington's disease: dominant, nerve damage later in life
Only one H allele is needed to be affected
teach.note: For Huntington's, Hh × hh gives 50% chance of an affected child. Mention genetic counselling kindly; do not make pupils feel their own families are being analysed. Link to protein shape from the previous lesson.

misconception.wrong: A carrier of cystic fibrosis has the disease.
misconception.right: A carrier has one recessive allele and does not have the disease. Two copies are needed.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils think a family with three girls is 'due' a boy.

check.q: A couple already have three daughters. What is the probability that their fourth child is a boy?
check.why: Each birth is independent, so the probability is 1 in 2.

practice: State which parent decides the sex of a child.
Explain what is meant by a carrier.
Give the genotype of someone with Huntington's disease who has one affected parent.
independent: Core: Draw a Punnett square for XX × XY and give the ratio.
Extend: A man with Huntington's disease (Hh) and an unaffected woman (hh) have a child. Give the probability of the child being affected. [2 marks]
Stretch: Draw a pedigree for a family where two unaffected parents have two affected children and one unaffected child; label genotypes. [4 marks]
exit: Define phenotype and genotype. [2 marks]

lessons.title: Mitosis, meiosis and chromosome numbers
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do you keep 46 chromosomes in every body cell but make gametes with only 23?
objectives: Describe mitosis and its roles
Describe meiosis and why it produces genetically different haploid gametes
Use chromosome numbers in diploid and haploid cells
successCriteria: All: state the outcomes of mitosis and meiosis
Most: compare the two processes and give chromosome numbers
Some: explain how meiosis and fertilisation create variation
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: powers of two
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on the order in cell division and life's continuity

keywords.def: cell with two sets of chromosomes (46 in humans)
cell with one set of chromosomes (23 in humans)
cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid cells
cell division that produces four genetically different haploid gametes

starter: Bismillah. What does a gamete contain?
State where DNA is stored in a human cell.

teach.heading: Mitosis
bullets: One division produces two identical daughter cells
Same chromosome number as the parent cell
Used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction
teach.note: DNA is copied first so each daughter cell gets a full set. Uncontrolled mitosis forms tumours (cancer).

teach.heading: Meiosis and variation
bullets: Halves the chromosome number: 46 to 23
Daughter cells are genetically different
Fertilisation restores diploid number
teach.note: Reasons for difference: chromosomes shuffle into gametes randomly. With 23 pairs there are over 8 million possible combinations in a single gamete (2²³). This is a stretch idea. Fertilisation joins two gametes, giving 46 chromosomes again, and increases variation.

model.problem: A horse body cell has 64 chromosomes. How many chromosomes in (a) a daughter cell after mitosis, (b) a horse gamete, (c) a zygote?

teach.heading: Checks and common errors
bullets: Mitosis makes identical cells
Meiosis makes unique gametes
Chromosome number halves only in meiosis
teach.note: Ask pupils to hold up 1 finger for mitosis, 2 for meiosis for each statement read aloud.

misconception.wrong: Meiosis produces gametes identical to each other and to the parent cell.
misconception.right: Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells, each with half the chromosome number.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils recall mitosis for 'growth' but forget gametes need meiosis.

check.q: Which process makes sperm cells in the testes?
check.why: Gametes are made by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number.

practice: How many chromosomes in a human skin cell and sperm cell?
Explain why gametes must be haploid.
State two uses of mitosis.
independent: Core: Make a comparison table of mitosis and meiosis.
Extend: A fruit fly has 8 chromosomes in a body cell. State the number in a gamete and zygote. [2 marks]
Stretch: Explain why siblings (other than identical twins) are not genetically identical. [3 marks]
exit: Define diploid and haploid. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: explain with numbers.
lessons.homework: Draw a diagram of a cell with 4 chromosomes dividing by mitosis and by meiosis.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: chromosome cards to physically sort. Stretch: how does non-disjunction cause Down syndrome?

lessons.title: Variation and mutation
lessons.bigQuestion: Why are no two people identical, even twins who share all their genes?
objectives: Distinguish genetic and environmental causes of variation
Describe continuous and discontinuous variation
Describe mutation as rare, random and inheritable and state what mutagens are
successCriteria: All: give examples of genetic and environmental variation
Most: describe mutation and mutagens
Some: explain the consequences of a mutation and interpret data
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: data handling and distributions
lessons.smsc: Moral: respect for human difference; avoiding unnecessary exposure to harm

keywords.def: differences between individuals of the same species
random change in the DNA sequence
agent that increases the rate of mutation, e.g. ionising radiation
passed on to offspring if the mutation is in the gametes

starter: Bismillah. Name the molecule that carries genetic information.
State the number of chromosomes in a human gamete.

teach.heading: Causes of variation
bullets: Genetic: different alleles from the parents
Environmental: diet, climate, accidents
Most features are influenced by both
teach.note: Examples: eye colour (genetic), scar (environmental), height (genes plus nutrition), skin tone (genes plus sunlight). Identical twins share genes, so differences between them are environmental. Illustrative class data: height of identical twins differs by about 1 cm, mass by 3 kg.

teach.heading: Mutation
bullets: A mutation changes the base sequence of a gene
Rare and random
Inherited only if it occurs in a gamete or the cell that forms gametes
teach.note: Most mutations are harmless or harmful; a few are beneficial. Mutagens raise the rate: ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, UV) and chemicals in tobacco smoke (Biology only). Link to cancer if mutations affect cell division genes.

model.problem: Explain how a mutation in the gene for an enzyme could stop the enzyme working. [3 marks]
steps: A different amino acid may be placed in the protein chain
The protein folds into a different shape
The active site no longer fits the substrate
model.answer: A changed base sequence can alter the active site shape

teach.heading: Interpreting variation data
bullets: Use mean, range and graphs
Look for overlapping distributions
Cause cannot be proved by a correlation alone
teach.note: Give a table of leaf lengths of ivy from sun and shade: e.g. sun mean 4.8 cm, shade mean 6.1 cm. Use as an environmental effect when plants are genetically identical.

misconception.wrong: A mutation is always harmful.
misconception.right: Most are neutral or harmful, but some are beneficial and can spread through a population.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils tick 'hair colour' for environmental because of dye.

check.q: Which is an example of discontinuous variation?
check.why: Blood group falls into distinct categories. Height, mass and foot length vary across a range.

practice: Give one genetic and one environmental cause of variation.
State two mutagens.
Explain why a mutation in a skin cell is not inherited.
independent: Core: Sort ten features into genetic, environmental or both.
Extend: Explain why identical twins raised apart can differ in mass but not blood group. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the statement 'all mutations are harmful'. [4 marks]
exit: Define mutation. [1 mark]
Return to the big question using the terms genes and environment.
lessons.homework: Collect data on a continuous and a discontinuous feature in your family (with permission) and present it.

lessons.title: Natural selection and antibiotic resistance
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a population change over generations, and why do some infections stop responding to treatment?
objectives: Describe Darwin's theory of natural selection in the stages the specification requires
Apply the theory to the peppered moth
Explain how antibiotic resistance develops in bacteria
successCriteria: All: list the stages of natural selection
Most: apply them to a population and to bacteria
Some: explain how data support selection and calculate bacterial growth
lessons.crossCurricular: Medicine: antibiotics; History of science
lessons.smsc: Intellectual honesty: describe the scientific theory accurately as the examination requires, weigh evidence, and respect differing views

keywords.def: process in which better-adapted individuals survive and pass on their alleles more often
feature that helps an organism survive in its environment
ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic
strain of bacteria resistant to many antibiotics

starter: Name the process by which bacteria reproduce.

teach.heading: Darwin's theory: stages
bullets: Individuals in a species show variation
More offspring are born than survive
Better-adapted individuals survive and reproduce, passing on their alleles
teach.note: Be exact: this is what the specification requires pupils to know and explain, and they must use these terms in the exam. Darwin proposed natural selection after observations and the work of others; the modern understanding adds genes and mutation as the source of new alleles. Teach the theory and its supporting evidence precisely; pupils may hold their own views and this lesson is about describing and explaining the scientific theory.
cycle: They reproduce and pass on alleles

teach.heading: Example: peppered moth
bullets: Pale and dark forms of Biston betularia
Industrial areas: soot darkened tree bark
Dark moths survived better; their allele became more common
teach.note: Records from Manchester show dark forms rose from rare in the mid-1800s to about 98% by 1895. After clean-air laws in the 20th century the pale form became common again. Predation by birds acted as the selective pressure.

model.problem: Explain how the dark form of the peppered moth became more common near industrial cities. [4 marks]
steps: There was variation: some moths were dark, some pale
Soot-covered bark made pale moths easier for birds to see
Dark moths survived and reproduced more
They passed on the dark allele, so it became more common
model.answer: Dark moths were better camouflaged, survived and passed on their allele

teach.heading: Antibiotic resistance
bullets: Bacteria vary because of random mutation
Antibiotic kills most bacteria; resistant ones survive
Survivors reproduce; population becomes resistant
teach.note: Maths: a bacterium divides every 20 minutes. After 2 hours there are 2⁶ = 64 cells; after 6 hours 2¹⁸ = 262 144. Resistance spreads because bacteria multiply quickly. Reduce risk: complete the course, do not use antibiotics for viral infections, avoid overuse.

misconception.wrong: Bacteria become resistant because the antibiotic makes them change on purpose.
misconception.right: Resistant bacteria arise by random mutation. The antibiotic selects them, because the others die.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: 'the bacteria got used to it' is the commonest wrong idea.

check.q: Which statement best explains why a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic?
options: Bacteria learn to resist the drug
The drug causes mutations in all bacteria
Antibiotics make bacteria multiply more slowly
check.why: Random mutation produces some resistant bacteria; the antibiotic kills the rest, so the resistant ones reproduce and pass on the allele.

practice: List the steps of natural selection in order.
State two ways to reduce antibiotic resistance.
Calculate the bacterial number after 3 hours if one cell divides every 20 minutes.
independent: Core: Describe the peppered moth case in five sentences using the terms variation, selection and allele.
Extend: Explain why MRSA is difficult to treat in hospitals. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the evidence for natural selection from the peppered moth. [4 marks]
exit: Define natural selection. [2 marks]
Return to the big question in your own words.

lessons.bigQuestion: How do we count the living world, and what does a number of species tell us?

Estimate a population from quadrat data
Describe how abiotic gradients explain the distribution of organisms along a transect

Most: calculate a population estimate and compare habitats
Some: interpret transect data and evaluate conclusions
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: fieldwork and human impact; Maths: sampling
lessons.smsc: Stewardship (khilafah): protecting the variety of species as an amanah

keywords.def: the number and variety of different species in an area
line across a habitat along which organisms are sampled
choosing sample positions by chance to avoid bias
where organisms are found

teach.heading: Biodiversity
bullets: More species means higher biodiversity
Species-rich habitats are usually more stable
Damage to a habitat often reduces species number
teach.note: Say clearly: this lesson extends the earlier quadrat lesson to biodiversity (Biology only) and distribution. Contrast a mown lawn (about 3 species) and an unmown meadow (over 12). Link back to food webs: more species gives more feeding links.

teach.heading: Sampling with quadrats
bullets: Place quadrats at random using coordinates
Count each species in every quadrat
Estimate = mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area)
teach.note: Random coordinates from a random number table or generator avoid choosing 'nice' spots. More quadrats make the mean more reliable. Biodiversity is the number of species found.

model.problem: A field has area 600 m². Ten quadrats of 0.25 m² contain these daisy counts: 4, 2, 5, 3, 6, 4, 3, 5, 2, 6. Estimate the population of daisies.

teach.heading: Distribution along a transect
bullets: Lay a tape from woodland edge into open grass
Quadrat every 5 m; measure light each time
Compare abundance with the abiotic factor
teach.note: Sample data: distance 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 m; shade-loving fern per m²: 22, 15, 8, 2, 0; relative light: 12, 25, 48, 80, 100. Pattern: fern decreases as light rises. Correlation suggests but does not prove cause; check soil moisture and pH as well.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils pick a link as proof; other abiotic factors might also change along the transect.

check.q: Fern numbers fall as light increases along a transect. What is the best conclusion?
options: Light could be a factor, but other factors should be checked
Ferns cannot live in the light
check.why: Correlation is not proof of cause. Moisture, soil and temperature may also vary along the transect.

practice: Define biodiversity.
Why are quadrat positions chosen at random?
A field of 400 m² has a mean of 5 plants per 1 m² quadrat. Estimate the population.
independent: Core: Calculate the mean and population estimate from the data your teacher gives for a 0.5 m² quadrat.
Extend: Explain why the meadow has higher biodiversity than the lawn. [3 marks]

exit: State two ways to make quadrat data more reliable. [2 marks]

c = 4.18 J/g/°C; ΔT = change in temperature

teach.note: Draw the diagram and mark Ea and ΔH. Example data: reactants at 0 kJ, peak +150 kJ, products at −80 kJ; Ea = 150 kJ, ΔH = −80 kJ. With a catalyst the peak is +70 kJ: Ea = 70 kJ; ΔH remains −80 kJ.

model.problem: A reaction profile has reactants at 0 kJ, a peak at +150 kJ and products at −80 kJ. A catalyst lowers the peak to +70 kJ. State Ea and ΔH with and without the catalyst.
model.answer: Ea 150 → 70 kJ; ΔH = −80 kJ in both cases

teach.heading: Practical: hydrogen peroxide
bullets: Measure oxygen volume in a gas syringe every 20 s
Catalysts: MnO₂, CuO, liver
Keep mass of catalyst, volume and concentration of peroxide the same

check.q: What effect does a catalyst have on a reaction?

keywords.def: reaction that can go in both directions, shown by ⇌
forward and backward rates equal; concentrations constant
relative amounts of reactants and products
no substances enter or leave

starter: Name the product of the Haber process.

teach.heading: Reversible reactions
bullets: Written with ⇌
Hydrated copper sulfate: blue ⇌ white + water
Ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride
teach.note: Heat blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate: it turns white, water is driven off; add water and it turns blue again, getting warm. One direction is endothermic, the reverse is exothermic by the same amount of energy.

teach.heading: Dynamic equilibrium
bullets: In a closed system the rates become equal
Concentrations stay constant
Reactions are still happening in both directions
teach.note: Use the analogy of an escalator with people walking down at the same rate as it carries them up: the person stays at the same height, but is still moving. Equilibrium is reached only in a closed system.

teach.heading: Changing conditions
bullets: Higher temperature favours the endothermic direction
Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles
Catalysts do not change the position
teach.note: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic forwards, with 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. High pressure moves the position to the right; high temperature moves it left but speeds up the rate. Industrial compromise: about 450 °C, 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst.

model.problem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is exothermic. Predict and explain the effect of increased pressure and of higher temperature on the yield of ammonia.
steps: Left side 4 moles of gas, right side 2 moles
Higher pressure favours fewer moles, so more ammonia
Higher temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, so less ammonia
model.answer: More ammonia at higher pressure; less at higher temperature

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: 'nothing is happening' is the typical misconception of dynamic equilibrium.

check.q: In a dynamic equilibrium:
options: Forward and backward rates are equal
check.why: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations are constant (not necessarily equal).

Methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol
Burn to form CO₂ and H₂O

Resource and renewability
Link to the context

Fermentation needs low temperature, so energy costs are lower

Overall suitable because raw materials are cheap and renewable

bullets: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) turns orange to green
Product is ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
Wine left open becomes vinegar by microbial oxidation

It uses a renewable raw material
It uses high temperature and pressure

acid that is only partially ionised in water

bullets: Methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic acids
Weak acids; ethanoic acid pH about 3 (0.1 mol/dm³)
React with metals, carbonates, alkalis like other acids

bullets: Alcohol + carboxylic acid ⇌ ester + water
Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst; warm
Ethanol + ethanoic acid → ethyl ethanoate

Used in flavourings, perfumes, solvents
Volatile, insoluble or slightly soluble in water

biodegradable polyester made by microorganisms

bullets: Two different monomers, each with two functional groups
Monomers join; a small molecule (water) is lost
Link types: amide (–CONH–) and ester (–COO–)
teach.note: Contrast with addition polymers: only one product and monomers have C=C. Use block diagrams: HO–[ ]–OH (diol) with HOOC–[ ]–COOH (diacid) → …–OOC–[ ]–COO–[ ]–… + H₂O. Nylon: diamine + dicarboxylic acid.

teach.heading: Addition v condensation
bullets: Addition: one monomer type with C=C; only polymer forms
Condensation: two functional groups per monomer; polymer + water
Properties vary with monomers
teach.note: PET, from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, is used in drinks bottles and polyester fabric.

teach.heading: Model: block diagram of a polyester

Represent diacid as HOOC–[ ]–COOH
Join with an ester link, remove H₂O

The monomers join by the ester link –COO–

Biodegradable; made from renewable resources
More expensive than oil-based plastics

water pushed aside by a submerged object, equal to its volume
the space an object takes up
a solid with no simple formula for its volume

ρ = m ÷ V

1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³

lessons.title: States of matter, changes of state and latent energy
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a pan of boiling water stay at 100 °C even though the hob keeps supplying energy?
objectives: Describe the arrangement and motion of particles in solids, liquids and gases
Describe changes of state
Interpret a heating curve using the idea of latent energy
successCriteria: All: describe particle arrangements in each state
Most: label a heating curve and name each change
Some: explain the plateau in terms of energy changing potential energy, not temperature
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: particle model; Geography: the water cycle
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the ordered behaviour of matter

keywords.def: solid becomes liquid at the melting point
liquid becomes gas throughout the liquid at the boiling point
liquid becomes gas at the surface at any temperature
energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature

starter: Bismillah. Name the three states of matter.
Explain why gases are easy to compress.

teach.heading: Particle models
bullets: Solid: fixed positions, vibrate, strong forces
Liquid: close together, slide past each other
Gas: far apart, move randomly at high speed
Density: solid and liquid high; gas low
teach.note: Use ball-bearing or marble diagrams. Ask which state has most kinetic energy and why gases have low density: particles are far apart. Link to compressibility of gases.

teach.heading: Changes of state
bullets: Melting and freezing at the melting point
Boiling and condensing at the boiling point
Sublimation: solid to gas directly
Energy is transferred, but the particle number stays the same
teach.note: Pupils use arrows to show transfers: heating gives energy in, cooling takes energy out. Mass is conserved in changes of state since only the arrangement changes.

teach.heading: Heating curve and latent energy
bullets: Temperature rises: particles gain kinetic energy
Plateau: energy breaks bonds (potential energy rises)
Temperature stays constant during a change of state
Cooling curves are the reverse
teach.note: Sketch a heating curve for ice at -20°C to steam. Ask: what happens to the energy input on the plateau? It increases the potential energy of the particles as they separate, so average kinetic energy and temperature are unchanged. Write 'latent' as 'hidden'.

model.problem: Describe and explain the shape of a heating curve for ice taken from -10°C to 120°C.
steps: Ice warms to 0°C: temperature rises, kinetic energy rises
Plateau at 0°C: melting; energy breaks bonds, no temperature change
Water warms to 100°C: temperature rises again
Plateau at 100°C: boiling; then steam warms above 100°C
model.answer: Two plateaus appear at the melting and boiling points; the flat sections are latent energy and the sloping sections are temperature rises

teach.heading: Check: boiling
bullets: Choose the best explanation
teach.note: Option A is the misconception that the energy disappears. Ask pupils to say where the energy goes.

check.q: During boiling, the temperature of water stays at 100°C because the energy supplied...
options: is used to separate the particles
check.why: The energy increases the potential energy as particles separate. The kinetic energy and temperature stay the same.

practice: Describe the arrangement of particles in a liquid.
State the difference between evaporation and boiling.
Explain why steam at 100°C causes worse burns than water at 100°C.
independent: Core: Draw and label a heating curve for water.
Extend: Describe how the particle model explains why a gas fills its container.
Stretch: Explain, using ideas of kinetic energy and potential energy, why evaporation cools a liquid.
exit: State what latent energy means.
Explain why the temperature does not change while a solid melts.
lessons.homework: Draw a flow diagram of the changes of state, annotated with the energy transfers, and write a paragraph on the plateau.

lessons.title: Specific heat capacity
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does the sea stay cool on a hot day while the sand burns your feet?
objectives: Define specific heat capacity
Use ΔQ = mcΔθ
Describe an experiment to measure specific heat capacity
successCriteria: All: state what specific heat capacity means
Most: use ΔQ = mcΔθ to find energy, mass or temperature change
Some: analyse experimental data and evaluate heat losses
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: sea breezes and climate; Maths: rearranging
lessons.smsc: Moral: careful and honest evaluation of experimental error

keywords.def: the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a material by 1 °C
energy transferred because of a temperature difference
final temperature minus initial temperature, Δθ
material used to reduce heat loss

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the energy transferred by a 60 W heater in 5.0 minutes.

teach.heading: What is specific heat capacity?
bullets: Different materials need different energy to warm up
c is the energy per kg per °C
Water: about 4200 J/kg°C; aluminium about 900 J/kg°C
High c: heats up slowly, cools slowly
teach.note: Link to the big question: water has a high c and also mixes and evaporates, so the sea warms slowly. Sand has a low c. Ask pupils to use units to remember: J per kg per °C.

model.problem: Calculate the energy needed to heat 2.0 kg of water from 20°C to 40°C (c = 4200 J/kg°C).

teach.heading: Core practical: finding c for a metal block
bullets: Insulated block with a heater and a thermometer in drilled holes
Record the starting temperature
Heat for 5 minutes with a joulemeter or measure V, I and t
Calculate c = E ÷ (m × Δθ)
teach.note: Independent variable: heating time; dependent: temperature; controls: mass of the block, insulation. Energy by E = IVt. Expected: temperature rises roughly linearly with energy; the gradient is 1/(mc). Heat losses mean the measured c is higher than the true value. Safety: the heater and block get hot; do not touch.

model.problem: A 0.50 kg aluminium block is heated by a 60 W heater for 5.0 minutes and its temperature rises by 40°C. Calculate its specific heat capacity.

teach.heading: Improving the experiment
bullets: Insulate the block to reduce losses
Add a little oil in the thermometer hole for good contact
Take the maximum temperature reached
Plot temperature against energy and use the gradient
teach.note: Ask pupils to explain what the result would be if a lot of heat was lost to the room: more energy was supplied than the block gained, so the calculated c is too high. Ask for improvements and their effect.

misconception.wrong: A material with a high specific heat capacity heats up quickly.
misconception.right: A high specific heat capacity means a lot of energy is needed for each degree, so it heats up slowly.

teach.heading: Check: rearranging
bullets: Select the answer
teach.note: Option B forgets mass. Option C multiplies where division is needed.

check.q: The energy needed to heat 0.50 kg of a liquid by 10°C is 10 500 J. What is c?
check.why: c = 10 500 ÷ (0.50 × 10) = 2100 J/kg°C. 1050 forgets that mass is 0.50 kg.

practice: Calculate the energy needed to heat 1.5 kg of water by 30°C (c = 4200 J/kg°C).
A 2.0 kg copper block (c = 390 J/kg°C) cools by 50°C. Calculate the energy released.
A 3.0 kW kettle heats 1.0 kg of water from 20°C. How long does it take to reach 80°C, ignoring heat loss?
independent: Core: State why a metal pan is made of a material with a low specific heat capacity.
Extend: 4.2 kJ heats a 0.20 kg block by 21°C. Calculate its specific heat capacity.
Stretch: A student finds c for a block is 1100 J/kg°C when the book value is 900. Explain the cause and suggest two improvements.
exit: Write the equation for the energy needed to change a temperature.
State what the units J/kg°C tell you.
lessons.homework: Write up the specific-heat-capacity experiment with a results table, an energy-temperature graph and an evaluation.
lessons.send: SEND: give a rearrangement triangle for ΔQ, m, c and Δθ. EAL: pre-teach capacity, insulate. Stretch: connect c to the particle model.

lessons.title: Gases: pressure, temperature and the Kelvin scale
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is it dangerous to put an aerosol can in a fire?
objectives: Explain gas pressure using the kinetic model
State absolute zero and convert between °C and K
Use p₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂ ÷ T₂ at constant volume
successCriteria: All: explain gas pressure by particle collisions
Most: convert °C to K and calculate pressure changes
Some: explain the temperature effect using particle speed and collision rate
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: kinetic theory; DT: pressure vessels
lessons.smsc: Moral: safe handling of pressurised containers and aerosols

keywords.def: gases are made of particles in constant random motion
the lowest possible temperature, 0 K or -273 °C
SI unit of temperature, T (K) = θ (°C) + 273
force per unit area from particles colliding with the walls

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for pressure.
Describe the motion of particles in a gas.

teach.heading: Why gases exert pressure
bullets: Particles move randomly and collide with the walls
Each collision gives a tiny force
Many collisions per second: steady pressure
Heating makes particles faster: more frequent, harder collisions
teach.note: Use a trolley or a model with ball bearings in a shaking tray. Ask: if you double the number of particles in the same volume, what happens to pressure? It increases. The container is not 'pushing outwards'; it is particles hitting walls.
cycle: Gas heated: particles gain kinetic energy
They hit the walls more often
Each collision exerts a greater force

teach.heading: Absolute zero and the Kelvin scale
bullets: Lowest possible temperature: -273°C = 0 K
Particles have minimum kinetic energy
A change of 1 K equals a change of 1°C
teach.note: Pressure falls linearly with temperature in a sealed container, and extrapolates to zero at -273°C. Stress that gas law calculations need kelvin, not Celsius. Typical error: using Celsius.

teach.heading: Pressure and temperature at constant volume
bullets: p₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂ ÷ T₂
Use kelvin for T
Pressure is proportional to the kelvin temperature
Volume and amount of gas are fixed
teach.note: Show a sealed flask with a pressure gauge in water baths. A graph of p against T (K) is a straight line through the origin. State it as p ∝ T.

model.problem: A sealed container of gas is at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 27°C. It is heated to 87°C. Calculate the new pressure.

teach.heading: Check: Celsius trap
bullets: Pick the right method
teach.note: Option A is the typical error of using Celsius. Option B adds instead of using a ratio.

check.q: A gas at 20°C is heated to 40°C at constant volume. Which statement about its pressure is correct?
check.why: Use kelvin: 20°C = 293 K, 40°C = 313 K. The ratio is 1.07, so pressure increases about 7%, not 100%.

practice: Convert -73°C and 127°C to kelvin.
A gas at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K is cooled to 150 K at constant volume. Calculate the new pressure.
Explain in terms of particles why a heated gas in a sealed container has a higher pressure.
independent: Core: Explain why an aerosol can must not be heated.
Extend: A car tyre has an air pressure of 2.2 × 10⁵ Pa at 10°C. After a long drive the temperature is 40°C. Calculate the new pressure, assuming a constant volume.
Stretch: Explain why the p-T graph for a gas extrapolates to zero pressure at -273°C, and why no real gas can reach absolute zero.
exit: State the value of absolute zero in °C and K.
State why temperatures must be in kelvin for p₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂ ÷ T₂.
lessons.homework: Make a leaflet warning about the dangers of leaving aerosol cans in a hot car, with the particle explanation and one calculation.
lessons.send: SEND: give a conversion card and a step table (convert, substitute, rearrange). EAL: pre-teach random, collide, absolute. Stretch: the link between temperature and average kinetic energy.

lessons.title: Gases: pressure and volume (Boyle's law)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a bubble get bigger as it rises from the bottom of a pool to the surface?
objectives: Explain why pressure increases when the volume of a gas decreases
Use p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ at constant temperature
Describe an experiment to investigate pressure and volume
successCriteria: All: explain the effect of compressing a gas
Most: use p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
Some: analyse p-V and p against 1/V graphs
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: inverse proportion; Diving: gas laws
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: appreciating how consistent patterns in nature allow safe technology such as diving and pumps

keywords.def: at constant temperature, pressure × volume is constant for a fixed mass of gas
squeezing a gas into a smaller volume
as one quantity increases, the other decreases at the same rate
temperature that stays the same during an investigation

starter: Bismillah. State why a heated gas in a sealed container has greater pressure.

teach.heading: Smaller volume, greater pressure
bullets: Same number of particles in a smaller space
Particles hit the walls more often
Pressure increases
At constant temperature, p × V = constant
teach.note: Use a syringe with the end sealed: pushing the plunger is harder as volume decreases. Ask pupils to say it in terms of collisions per second per unit area. Temperature must stay constant: compress slowly.

model.problem: A gas of volume 120 cm³ is at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. It is compressed to 40 cm³ at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure.

teach.heading: Core practical: pressure and volume
bullets: Syringe connected to a pressure gauge
Trapped air: record volume and pressure
Compress or expand slowly in steps; wait for temperature to settle
Plot p against 1/V: a straight line through the origin
teach.note: Independent variable: volume; dependent: pressure; control: temperature and mass of gas. Expected: p ∝ 1/V; pV roughly constant. Safety: keep within the syringe's pressure limit; eye protection is advisable. Slow movements keep the temperature constant.

check.q: In a syringe experiment, a student plots p against 1/V. What shape should the graph be?
options: a straight line through the origin
a straight line with a negative gradient
check.why: p ∝ 1/V, so p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin. A p-V graph is a curve.

teach.heading: Rising bubbles
bullets: Pressure falls as the bubble rises
So its volume increases
Using p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ gives the new volume
Pressure at depth includes atmospheric pressure
teach.note: Use absolute pressure: at 10 m under water the pressure is about 2 atmospheres (2.0 × 10⁵ Pa). Link back to the big question. Safety link: divers must exhale on ascent to avoid lung over-expansion.

model.problem: A bubble of 2.0 cm³ at the bottom of a pool has pressure 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. At the surface the pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate its volume there, assuming constant temperature.

teach.heading: Common errors
bullets: Using Celsius values or mixing units
Forgetting that the temperature must be constant
Using gauge pressure instead of total pressure
teach.note: Remind pupils that Boyle's law needs constant temperature and mass; the Kelvin law needs constant volume. Ask them to label each law with its constants.

misconception.wrong: When a gas is compressed, its pressure doubles whenever the volume is halved, whatever the temperature.
misconception.right: Pressure doubles when the volume halves only if the temperature and amount of gas stay constant.

practice: A gas has pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and volume 600 cm³. It is compressed to 150 cm³. Calculate the new pressure.
A gas of volume 2.0 m³ at 5.0 × 10⁴ Pa expands to 5.0 m³. Calculate the new pressure.
Explain in terms of particles why the pressure rises when a gas is compressed.
independent: Core: Describe how to investigate how the pressure of a gas varies with volume.
Extend: A bicycle pump holds 400 cm³ of air at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. The air is compressed into 50 cm³ in the tyre. Calculate the pressure.
Stretch: A diver breathes out a bubble of 5.0 cm³ at 20 m depth where p = 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate its volume at the surface and explain the safety lesson for ascent.
exit: State the equation for Boyle's law.
State the condition needed for Boyle's law.
lessons.homework: Complete a summary table of the two gas laws: variables kept constant, equation, graph shape and particle explanation.
lessons.send: SEND: give the two-law summary table with gaps. EAL: pre-teach compress, expand, constant. Stretch: combine laws as p₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂V₂ ÷ T₂.

lessons.title: Magnets and magnetic fields
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a compass find north, and why does a magnet attract a paperclip but not a plastic ruler?
objectives: Describe the forces between magnetic poles and the shape of magnetic fields
Distinguish magnetically hard and soft materials
Explain induced magnetism
successCriteria: All: draw the field around a bar magnet with arrows
Most: describe how to plot a field with a compass and distinguish hard from soft
Some: explain induced magnetism and why a magnet always attracts iron
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: navigation and the Earth's field; History: the compass in Muslim and world navigation
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the invisible order of the world around us

keywords.def: the region around a magnet where a magnetic material feels a force
easily magnetised and demagnetised, e.g. iron
hard to magnetise but keeps its magnetism, e.g. steel
a magnetic material becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field

starter: Bismillah. State two properties of a magnet that you know.
Name the particles that carry current in a wire.
State what is meant by like charges repel.

teach.heading: Poles and fields
bullets: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract
Field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole
Closer lines mean a stronger field
Between two unlike poles: nearly uniform field
teach.note: Show iron filings and plotting compasses. Draw the pattern for a bar magnet, two unlike poles facing each other and two like poles. Explain the neutral point between like poles where the field is zero. The only certain test for a magnet is repulsion.

head: Arrangement
Field pattern
rows: curved lines from N to S, strongest at the poles
straight parallel lines between: uniform field
lines pushed apart; a neutral point in the middle

teach.heading: Core practical: plotting a field
bullets: Place a bar magnet on paper
Put a small plotting compass near the north pole
Mark both ends of the compass needle, then move it along
Join the marks to draw a field line
teach.note: Pupils draw at least four field lines. Variables: not an investigation of variables, but a technique: keep the magnet fixed, and keep other magnets and iron away. Earth's field makes a compass needle align north-south; the Earth's geographic north is near a magnetic south pole.

model.problem: Describe how to plot a magnetic field line of a bar magnet using a plotting compass.
steps: Place the magnet on paper; put the compass near the north pole
Mark dots at both ends of the compass needle
Move the compass so its tail sits on the previous front dot; mark again
Repeat until you reach the south pole, then join the dots with a smooth line
model.answer: A smooth curve from the north pole to the south pole shows one field line; repeat from other starting points

teach.heading: Hard and soft materials; induced magnetism
bullets: Soft (iron): magnetised easily, loses magnetism quickly: electromagnets
Hard (steel): keeps its magnetism: permanent magnets
Iron near a magnet becomes a temporary magnet
The induced pole nearest is opposite: so always attracted
teach.note: Show a paperclip chain hanging from a magnet: each clip is magnetised by induction. Ask why a magnet attracts both ends of a paperclip: it creates an opposite pole nearest to it. Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic; plastics, wood and aluminium are not.

misconception.wrong: A magnet can attract and repel an unmagnetised iron bar.
misconception.right: A magnet only attracts unmagnetised iron, because it induces an opposite pole nearest to the magnet. Repulsion only happens with another magnet.

teach.heading: Check: testing for a magnet
bullets: Select the best test
teach.note: Option A confuses attraction with magnetism, as induced magnetism also attracts. Pupils should justify the answer.

check.q: A rod is attracted to the north pole of a magnet and also attracted to the south pole. What can you conclude?
options: The rod is unmagnetised iron or steel
The rod is made of plastic
The rod is a south pole
check.why: A magnet would repel one of the poles. Attraction to both means the rod is a magnetic material, but not a magnet.

practice: Draw the field around a bar magnet, using arrows.
Explain why steel is used for permanent magnets and iron for electromagnets.
A student brings a magnet near an iron nail and the nail picks up paperclips. Explain why.
independent: Core: Describe how to plot the magnetic field of a bar magnet.
Extend: Sketch the field between the north pole of one magnet and the north pole of another and mark the neutral point.
Stretch: Explain, using induced magnetism, why a magnet can lift a chain of paperclips and why the chain collapses when the magnet is removed.
exit: State the direction of field lines outside a magnet.
Define magnetically soft.
lessons.homework: Draw and label three field patterns (bar magnet, two unlike poles, two like poles) and write one sentence under each.
lessons.send: SEND: use a pre-drawn dot grid for field plotting. EAL: pre-teach pole, attract, repel, induced. Stretch: describe the Earth's magnetic field and how it protects against charged particles.

lessons.title: Electromagnets: the magnetic field of a current
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a magnet be switched on and off, and why is that useful for lifting scrap metal?
objectives: Describe the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire and a solenoid
State factors that affect the strength of an electromagnet
Describe uses of electromagnets including a relay
successCriteria: All: state that a current produces a magnetic field
Most: describe the field patterns and the factors affecting strength
Some: explain how a relay or electric bell works
lessons.crossCurricular: DT: electromagnetic devices; Engineering: recycling plants
lessons.smsc: Moral: using science to improve everyday safety

keywords.def: a long coil of wire carrying a current, with a field like a bar magnet
a solenoid with an iron core that can be switched on and off
a switch operated by an electromagnet
the iron placed inside a solenoid to strengthen the field

starter: Bismillah. Describe the field pattern of a bar magnet.

teach.heading: Current produces a magnetic field
bullets: A current in a wire makes a circular field around the wire
Reversing the current reverses the field direction
The field is stronger with greater current and nearer the wire
A solenoid gives a field like a bar magnet
teach.note: Demonstrate with a vertical wire through card and plotting compasses, or iron filings. Direction of the field around a wire can be found with the right-hand grip rule (thumb along the current, fingers curl along the field). Check the specification for how the direction is examined.

left.title: Straight wire
points: Reverse the current: reverses the field

right.title: Solenoid
points: Field inside is strong and uniform
Ends act as north and south poles

teach.heading: Strengthening an electromagnet
bullets: Increase the current
Add more turns of wire
Insert a soft iron core
Soft iron loses magnetism when the current stops
teach.note: Practical: electromagnet picking up paperclips; independent variable: current (or turns); dependent: number of paperclips; controls: core, turns, same clips. Safety: wires and coils warm up; switch off between readings. Expected: more current and more turns lift more clips.

model.problem: Describe how you would investigate how the strength of an electromagnet depends on the number of turns.
steps: Wind the wire round an iron nail; use 10 turns
Connect it to a fixed current from a power supply
Count the paperclips the nail can pick up
Repeat with 20, 30, 40 turns and plot clips against turns
model.answer: The number of paperclips should increase as the number of turns increases, for a constant current

teach.heading: Uses: relay and bell
bullets: A small current switches a large current
Relay: electromagnet pulls an iron armature to close a second circuit
Electric bell: the armature breaks the circuit, so it vibrates repeatedly
Scrapyard crane: strong electromagnet switched off to release the load
teach.note: Walk through the relay on the board: control circuit, electromagnet, soft iron armature, switch contacts, high-current circuit. Ask pupils why a relay is useful for safety: a low-voltage switch can control a mains device.
cycle: Small current switches on the electromagnet in the control circuit
The electromagnet attracts the iron armature
The armature closes the contacts of the second circuit
A large current flows through the device
Current off: armature springs back and the circuit opens

teach.heading: Check: electromagnet
bullets: Choose the factor
teach.note: Option C is the common misconception that the current direction affects the strength. Option D is not a factor for strength.

check.q: Which change would NOT make an electromagnet stronger?
options: reversing the direction of the current
check.why: Reversing the current reverses the poles but does not change the strength.

practice: State three ways to increase the strength of an electromagnet.
Explain why soft iron rather than steel is used for the core of an electromagnet in a crane.
Describe the field pattern around a solenoid.
independent: Core: Describe how a relay allows a small current to switch a large current.
Extend: Explain how an electric bell works using an electromagnet and a spring contact.
Stretch: Explain why a coil with an iron core still lifts paperclips after the current is switched off if the core is steel, but not if it is iron.
exit: State what happens to the field when the current is reversed.
Name one use of an electromagnet.

lessons.send: SEND: give a relay diagram with a word bank. EAL: pre-teach solenoid, armature, core. Stretch: investigate how field strength inside a solenoid varies with current.

Explain how a d.c. motor works
Explain how a loudspeaker works

keywords.def: a force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field
a rule to find force direction from field and current direction
a split ring that reverses the current every half turn
a device that uses the motor effect to make a cone vibrate

starter: Bismillah. State the direction of field lines outside a magnet.
Name two ways to strengthen an electromagnet.
State the direction of conventional current.

teach.heading: The motor effect
bullets: A wire carrying current in a magnetic field feels a force
Force is greatest when the wire is at 90° to the field
No force when the wire is parallel to the field
Reversing the current or the field reverses the force
teach.note: Use a wire on a rail between magnets, or a jumping wire. The interaction is between the wire's field and the magnet's field. Increase the force: bigger current, stronger magnets.

model.problem: A wire carrying current out of the page lies in a field pointing from left to right. Use the left-hand rule to find the direction of the force.
steps: First finger: field, pointing to the right
Second finger: conventional current, pointing out of the page towards you
The thumb is at right angles to both
Thumb points upwards: the force is up the page
model.answer: The force on the wire is upwards

teach.heading: The d.c. motor
bullets: A coil in a magnetic field with current
Forces on opposite sides act in opposite directions
Coil rotates; commutator reverses the current each half turn
Keeps the rotation continuing in one direction
teach.note: Draw the coil, magnets, split-ring commutator and carbon brushes. Ask what would happen without the commutator: the coil would flip back and forth and stop. To change speed: more current, stronger magnets, more turns. Reverse direction: swap the battery or magnets.

head: Part
Job
rows: keep contact with the rotating commutator

teach.heading: The loudspeaker
bullets: Coil attached to a paper cone sits in a permanent magnet's field
Alternating current from the amplifier flows in the coil
Force on the coil moves it in and out
The cone vibrates the air, producing sound of the same frequency
teach.note: Show a speaker with the cover removed. Ask: how does a higher-frequency signal change the sound? (Faster vibration, higher pitch; larger current gives larger amplitude, louder.)

misconception.wrong: The loudspeaker cone is moved by static electricity.
misconception.right: A loudspeaker uses the motor effect: alternating current in the coil in a magnetic field makes the cone vibrate at the signal's frequency.

teach.heading: Check: left-hand rule
bullets: Pick the answer
teach.note: Remind pupils that the second finger is the current direction. The most common error is mixing the field and current.

check.q: What happens to the force on a wire if both the current and the field are reversed?
options: It stays in the same direction
check.why: Each reversal reverses the force, so reversing both gives the original direction.

practice: State three ways to increase the speed of a d.c. motor.
Explain why a motor needs a commutator.
Explain what happens to a loudspeaker cone when the signal's frequency increases.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic induction and generators
lessons.bigQuestion: How can moving a magnet near a coil make electricity without any battery?
objectives: Describe electromagnetic induction
State what affects the size and direction of the induced voltage
Explain how an a.c. generator works
successCriteria: All: state that relative motion of a magnet and coil induces a voltage
Most: state factors increasing induced voltage
Some: explain the output graph of a simple a.c. generator
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: power stations; DT: dynamos on bicycles
lessons.smsc: Moral: appreciating those whose discoveries benefit all of humanity

keywords.def: generating a voltage in a conductor when it cuts magnetic field lines or the field changes
a device that transfers kinetic energy to electrical energy
rings that keep contact with a rotating coil to give a.c. output
a small generator, such as on a bicycle

starter: Bismillah. State two ways to increase the speed of a motor.
State the difference between a.c. and d.c.
Name the energy transfer in a generator.

teach.heading: Induced voltage
bullets: Move a magnet into or out of a coil: a voltage is induced
No movement: no voltage
Reverse the movement: voltage reverses
Same effect if the wire moves across the field
teach.note: Use a coil connected to a sensitive voltmeter or galvanometer. Move the magnet in, hold, out. The needle deflects only while the magnet moves. Ask: what if the coil moves instead? Same result. Voltage is induced when the field lines are cut.

model.problem: A bar magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a sensitive voltmeter and then pulled out. Describe what you see.
steps: Magnet moves in: the voltmeter deflects one way
Magnet stationary in the coil: no reading
Magnet pulled out: the voltmeter deflects the opposite way
model.answer: A voltage appears only when the magnet moves, and reverses when the direction of movement reverses

teach.heading: Increasing the induced voltage
bullets: Move the magnet or coil faster
Use a stronger magnet
Use more turns of wire
Use a coil with a larger area
teach.note: Pupils recall these with a mnemonic. Link to energy: the energy comes from the work done moving the magnet against the opposing field. Ask pupils to design an experiment to test one factor.

teach.heading: The a.c. generator
bullets: A coil spins in a magnetic field
Slip rings and brushes connect it to the outside circuit
Voltage reverses every half turn: a.c.
Faster rotation: higher frequency and bigger amplitude
teach.note: Sketch the output graph as a sine curve. At the vertical position the coil cuts the field fastest, so the voltage is at its peak; when horizontal, no lines are cut and the voltage is zero. A power station generator is the same idea with electromagnets and many turns.

check.q: A generator's coil is rotated twice as fast. The output voltage has...
options: the same frequency and same peak
a higher frequency and a higher peak voltage
a lower frequency and a higher peak voltage
the same frequency and a higher peak
check.why: Faster rotation cuts field lines faster, so the peak voltage rises, and more cycles occur each second, so the frequency rises.

teach.heading: Motor effect versus induction
bullets: Motor: current and field give movement
Generator: movement and field give current
Same components, opposite energy transfer
teach.note: Ask pupils to complete the sentence: a motor transfers ___ energy to ___ energy; a generator transfers ___ to ___. Misconception: mixing the two devices.

misconception.wrong: A generator needs a battery to produce electricity.
misconception.right: A generator needs motion. Moving a coil in a magnetic field, such as by a turbine, induces a voltage with no battery.

practice: List three ways to increase the voltage induced in a coil by a moving magnet.
State what happens to the reading when a magnet is held still inside a coil.
Explain why a bicycle dynamo lamp gets brighter as the cyclist speeds up.
independent: Core: Describe the main parts of an a.c. generator.
Extend: Sketch a voltage-time graph for a generator, then sketch the effect of doubling the rotation speed.
Stretch: Explain, using energy ideas, why it is harder to pedal when a bicycle dynamo is connected to a lamp.
exit: State the energy transfer in a generator.
State how the induced voltage changes when the magnet moves faster.
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled diagram of an a.c. generator and write the steps to produce one cycle of output.
lessons.send: SEND: give a labelled generator diagram to cut and sequence. EAL: pre-teach induced, slip rings, cut field lines. Stretch: explain Lenz's law qualitatively.

lessons.title: Transformers and the National Grid
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is electricity sent across the country at hundreds of thousands of volts when our homes use 230 V?
objectives: Describe how a transformer works
Use Vₚ ÷ Vₛ = nₚ ÷ nₛ and Vₚ × Iₚ = Vₛ × Iₛ
Explain why the National Grid uses high voltage transmission
successCriteria: All: state the parts of a transformer and that it needs a.c.
Most: use the turns-ratio equation
Some: explain energy losses in transmission lines using power equations
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: energy supply networks; Maths: ratios
lessons.smsc: Moral: using resources efficiently for the benefit of communities

keywords.def: a device that changes the voltage of an a.c. supply
has more turns on the secondary coil, so increases voltage
has fewer turns on the secondary coil, so decreases voltage
the network of cables and transformers that carries electricity across the UK

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the power of a device with 230 V and 5.0 A.
State why a transformer cannot use d.c.

teach.heading: How a transformer works
bullets: Primary coil and secondary coil on a soft iron core
a.c. in the primary makes a changing magnetic field in the core
The changing field induces a voltage in the secondary
d.c. does not work: the field does not change
teach.note: Draw the core as a closed loop of soft iron with two coils. Ask: why does a d.c. supply give no output? (The field is constant so there is no induction.) Remind pupils that transformers change voltage, not power.

model.problem: A transformer has 1000 turns on its primary coil and 50 turns on its secondary. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.

teach.heading: Power in an ideal transformer
bullets: No energy lost: power in = power out
Vₚ × Iₚ = Vₛ × Iₛ
Step up the voltage: the current is stepped down
Real transformers are 90% to 99% efficient
teach.note: Link to the conservation of energy. Ask: if the voltage goes up 20 times, what happens to the current? It falls by a factor of 20.

model.problem: An ideal transformer steps 230 V down to 11.5 V. The secondary current is 2.0 A. Calculate the primary current.

teach.heading: The National Grid
bullets: Power stations generate at about 25 kV
Step-up transformers raise the voltage (up to 400 kV)
High voltage means low current for the same power
Low current: less heating in the cables, so less energy wasted
Step-down transformers near homes reduce the voltage to 230 V
teach.note: Use the power-loss calculation: P(loss) = I²R, derived from P = IV and V = IR (I × IR). Make the comparison explicit with the numbers in the model. Ask: why not just use thick cables? Cost and weight of copper.

model.problem: A power line delivers 100 kW. The cable resistance is 2.0 Ω. Compare the power lost as heat when transmitting at 1000 V and at 10 000 V.
steps: Ten times the voltage means 100 times less power lost
model.answer: Loss = 20 kW at 1000 V but only 200 W at 10 000 V

teach.heading: Check: step-up
bullets: Select the correct answer
teach.note: Option A reverses the coils. Option C ignores the effect on current.

check.q: A step-up transformer used in the National Grid...
options: has more turns on the primary than the secondary
increases the voltage and decreases the current
increases the voltage and the current
check.why: A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary, so the voltage rises while the current falls, keeping power almost constant.

practice: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary and 800 on the secondary. The input is 12 V. Calculate the output voltage.
A 24 V to 6.0 V transformer has a primary current of 0.50 A. Calculate the secondary current (ideal transformer).
Explain why transformers do not work with d.c.
independent: Core: Explain why electricity is transmitted at high voltage.
Extend: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 25 on the secondary. Calculate the output when the input is 230 V, and the secondary current if the primary current is 0.20 A.
Stretch: A 5.0 MW supply is transmitted down a line of total resistance 4.0 Ω at 250 kV. Calculate the current and the percentage of power lost.
exit: State the turns-ratio equation.
State one reason for using step-down transformers near homes.
lessons.homework: Draw the National Grid flow diagram from power station to home and explain the voltage changes at each stage.
lessons.send: SEND: give a flow-diagram template for the National Grid with sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach primary, secondary, transmit. Stretch: explain why real transformers are not perfectly efficient (eddy currents, resistance).

lessons.title: Atomic structure, nuclear notation and isotopes
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes carbon-12 and carbon-14 the same element but different atoms?
objectives: Describe the structure of the atom and the properties of protons, neutrons and electrons
Use atomic number, mass number and nuclear notation
Define isotopes and compare their structure
successCriteria: All: label protons, neutrons and electrons
Most: work out numbers of each particle from nuclear notation
Some: compare isotopes and explain why they have the same chemical properties
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: atoms and the Periodic Table; History of science: developing the model of the atom
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the order found even at the smallest scales of creation

keywords.def: the number of protons in the nucleus (Z)
the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus (A)
atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
a proton or a neutron

starter: Bismillah. State the charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
Describe the particles in the nucleus.

teach.heading: Inside the atom
bullets: Tiny dense nucleus of protons and neutrons
Electrons orbit the nucleus
Relative charges: proton +1, neutron 0, electron -1
Relative masses: proton 1, neutron 1, electron about 1/1840
Atoms are neutral: protons = electrons
teach.note: Draw a nuclear atom. Stress the scale: an atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m across, the nucleus around 10⁻¹⁵ m, so most of the atom is empty space. Link to the Rutherford scattering model if time allows. Atoms are neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

teach.heading: Nuclear notation
bullets: Written as ᴬ_Z X
A = mass number (protons + neutrons)
Z = atomic number (protons)
Neutrons = A - Z
teach.note: Write ¹⁴₆C on the board and read it aloud: carbon with atomic number 6 and mass number 14. Check that pupils find neutrons as A − Z. The element symbol alone tells you Z, but is written for clarity.

model.problem: Carbon-14 is written ¹⁴₆C. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom.

teach.heading: Isotopes
bullets: Same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons
Same chemical properties (same electrons)
Different masses and sometimes different stability
Some isotopes are radioactive
teach.note: Compare carbon-12 and carbon-14 using a table. Ask: why do they react the same way? Because chemistry depends on the electrons. Nuclei with the wrong neutron-to-proton balance are unstable and decay.

teach.heading: Check: isotopes
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option A confuses isotopes and ions. Option D is the common slip: mass number versus atomic number.

check.q: Which statement about isotopes of the same element is correct?
options: They have different numbers of protons
They have different numbers of neutrons
They have different numbers of electrons
check.why: Isotopes have the same atomic number (protons) but a different number of neutrons, and hence a different mass number.

practice: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in ²³₁₁Na.
Uranium-235 and uranium-238 both have 92 protons. State the number of neutrons in each.
Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
independent: Core: Copy and complete: particle / relative charge / relative mass for protons, neutrons and electrons.
Extend: An ion has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons. Write its nuclear notation, mass number and charge.
Stretch: Explain why alpha particles in the Rutherford experiment were mostly undeflected but a few bounced back, linking to the structure of the atom.
exit: Define atomic number and mass number.
State the number of neutrons in ¹⁴₆C.
lessons.homework: Make a table of three elements with their protons, neutrons, electrons and symbols using nuclear notation, plus one isotope for each.
lessons.send: SEND: give a notation template with arrows pointing to A, Z, symbol. EAL: pre-teach nucleus, nucleon, isotope. Stretch: explain why nuclei with too many neutrons are unstable.
